blocks.text: Definition

runs.t: Definition

blocks.text: Materials that allow electric charges to flow through them easily are called conductors.

runs.t: Materials that allow electric charges to flow through them easily are called conductors.

blocks.text: In conductors, some electrons are loosely bound to atoms and can move freely within the material. These free electrons are responsible for electrical conduction.

runs.t: In conductors, some electrons are loosely bound to atoms and can move freely within the material. These free electrons are responsible for electrical conduction.

blocks.text: Scientific Principle

runs.t: Scientific Principle

blocks.text: Metals contain a large number of free electrons. When a potential difference is applied across a conductor, these electrons move in a particular direction, resulting in the flow of electric current.

runs.t: Metals contain a large number of free electrons. When a potential difference is applied across a conductor, these electrons move in a particular direction, resulting in the flow of electric current.

blocks.text: Thus, electrical conduction in conductors occurs due to the movement of free electrons.

blocks.text: Lightning – A Large-Scale Electrical Discharge in the Atmosphere

runs.t: Lightning – A Large-Scale Electrical Discharge in the Atmosphere

blocks.text: Lightning is a natural electrical phenomenon produced by the accumulation and sudden discharge of electric charges inside clouds or between clouds and the Earth. It is one of the largest natural examples of static electricity.

runs.t: Lightning is a natural electrical phenomenon produced by the accumulation and sudden discharge of electric charges inside clouds or between clouds and the Earth. It is one of the largest natural examples of static electricity.

blocks.text: During thunderstorms, strong air currents continuously move water droplets, ice crystals, and hail particles inside clouds. Frequent collisions and friction between these particles produce electric charges.

runs.t: During thunderstorms, strong air currents continuously move water droplets, ice crystals, and hail particles inside clouds. Frequent collisions and friction between these particles produce electric charges.

blocks.text:
As a result:
• The upper part of the cloud generally becomes positively charged.
• The lower part becomes negatively charged.
• Sometimes a small positively charged region forms near the bottom of the cloud.

runs.t:
As a result:
• The upper part of the cloud generally becomes positively charged.
• The lower part becomes negatively charged.
• Sometimes a small positively charged region forms near the bottom of the cloud.

blocks.text: The negatively charged lower region of the cloud induces positive charges on the Earth’s surface directly below it due to electrical induction.

runs.t: The negatively charged lower region of the cloud induces positive charges on the Earth’s surface directly below it due to electrical induction.

blocks.text: Normally, air acts as an insulator and prevents the movement of charges. However, when the amount of charge becomes extremely large, the potential difference between oppositely charged regions increases enormously. At this stage, the insulating property of air breaks down. The air becomes ionised and suddenly allows electric current to pass through it.

runs.t: Normally, air acts as an insulator and prevents the movement of charges. However, when the amount of charge becomes extremely large, the potential difference between oppositely charged regions increases enormously. At this stage, the insulating property of air breaks down. The air becomes ionised and suddenly allows electric current to pass through it.

blocks.text: This sudden and rapid discharge of electricity produces a bright flash called lightning.

runs.t: This sudden and rapid discharge of electricity produces a bright flash called lightning.

blocks.text: The electric discharge heats the surrounding air to extremely high temperatures, sometimes close to 30,000°C. The heated air expands very rapidly and produces shock waves. These shock waves are heard as thunder.

runs.t: The electric discharge heats the surrounding air to extremely high temperatures, sometimes close to 30,000°C. The heated air expands very rapidly and produces shock waves. These shock waves are heard as thunder.

blocks.text: Light travels much faster than sound.

blocks.text: Lightning Conductor

runs.t: Lightning Conductor

blocks.text: A lightning conductor is a protective device used to safeguard buildings and tall structures from the damaging effects of lightning. It was developed by Benjamin Franklin after he demonstrated that lightning is an electrical discharge.

runs.t: A lightning conductor is a protective device used to safeguard buildings and tall structures from the damaging effects of lightning. It was developed by Benjamin Franklin after he demonstrated that lightning is an electrical discharge.

blocks.text:
A lightning conductor consists of:
• A long, thick metal rod, usually made of copper or aluminium
• A pointed upper end fixed at the highest point of the building
• A thick metal strip connected to the rod and extending down the side of the building
• A metal plate buried deep inside the ground

runs.t:
A lightning conductor consists of:
• A long, thick metal rod, usually made of copper or aluminium
• A pointed upper end fixed at the highest point of the building
• A thick metal strip connected to the rod and extending down the side of the building
• A metal plate buried deep inside the ground

blocks.text: The metal rod and strip provide a low-resistance conducting path between the atmosphere and the Earth.

runs.t: The metal rod and strip provide a low-resistance conducting path between the atmosphere and the Earth.

blocks.text: Working Principle of a Lightning Conductor

runs.t: Working Principle of a Lightning Conductor

blocks.text: During a thunderstorm, a large potential difference develops between the charged clouds and the Earth. If lightning strikes the building, the electric charge passes through the metal conductor directly into the ground instead of flowing through the building structure.

runs.t: During a thunderstorm, a large potential difference develops between the charged clouds and the Earth. If lightning strikes the building, the electric charge passes through the metal conductor directly into the ground instead of flowing through the building structure.

blocks.text:
Thus, the lightning conductor safely transfers the enormous electric charge to the Earth and protects the building from:
• Fire hazards
• Structural damage
• Electrical damage
• Risk to human life

runs.t:

blocks.text: Answer: Conductors are materials that allow electric charges to flow through them easily (e.g., copper, aluminium). Insulators are materials that do not allow electric charges to pass through them (e.g., wood, plastic). Conductors are used for making wires, while insulators are used for covering wires to prevent shocks.

blocks.text: 30. What is lightning? How does a lightning conductor protect a building from damage?

runs.t: What is lightning? How does a lightning conductor protect a building from damage?

blocks.text: Answer: Lightning is a huge electric spark caused by the sudden discharge of a large amount of electric charge accumulated in the clouds. A lightning conductor is a thick metal strip with a sharp pointed top fixed on buildings. It provides an easy path for the charge to flow safely into the ground, protecting the building from damage.

blocks.text: 31. Explain the working of an electric fuse. Why is it called a safety device?

runs.t: Explain the working of an electric fuse. Why is it called a safety device?

blocks.text: Answer: An electric fuse contains a thin wire of low melting point. When current exceeds the safe limit, the wire gets heated, melts, and breaks the circuit. This stops the flow of excess current and protects the appliance and wiring from damage. It is called a safety device because it prevents fire and damage due to overloading or short circuit.

blocks.text: When the switch is pressed, current flows through the coil and the electromagnet attracts the soft iron strip. The hammer strikes the gong and produces sound. At the same time, the strip loses contact with the screw, breaking the circuit. The electromagnet loses its magnetism and the strip returns to its original position due to the spring. This again completes the circuit. The process repeats rapidly, so the bell keeps ringing continuously as long as the switch is pressed.
